overview: Cerebrospinal fluid (CSF) is produced mainly by the choroid plexuses of the lateral, third, and fourth ventricles, circulates through the ventricular system (lateral → interventricular foramina → third ventricle → cerebral aqueduct → fourth ventricle), exits into the subarachnoid space via the median and lateral apertures, and is reabsorbed into the dural venous sinuses through arachnoid granulations. The system provides mechanical buoyancy, maintains ionic homeostasis, and is the conduit for the recently recognized glymphatic clearance of metabolic waste.

citations.source: Kandel et al., Principles of Neural Science, 6th ed. (2021), Ch. 3 (App. D)
Brodal, The Central Nervous System, 5th ed. (2016), Ch. 5

function: Specialized secretory epithelium (modified ependyma over a vascular stroma) that produces the majority of cerebrospinal fluid (~500 mL/day; total CSF volume ~150 mL).
Actively secretes CSF via ion transport (Na+/K+-ATPase, carbonic anhydrase) and forms the blood–CSF barrier.

clinical.note: Can overproduce CSF, causing communicating hydrocephalus.
Acetazolamide (carbonic anhydrase inhibition) reduces CSF production in idiopathic intracranial hypertension.

function: The paired largest ventricles (frontal horn, body, atrium, temporal & occipital horns), lined with choroid plexus in the body and inferior horn.
Serve as the principal CSF reservoir from which fluid flows into the third ventricle.

efferent: Third ventricle via the interventricular foramina of Monro

clinical.note: Obstruction (e.g., colloid cyst at the foramen of Monro) causes lateral-ventricle enlargement; the Evans index quantifies ventriculomegaly.

function: Narrow midline ventricle of the diencephalon receiving CSF from both lateral ventricles.
Its walls contain circumventricular organs (e.g., subfornical organ) and hypothalamic nuclei that sample CSF signals.

efferent: Fourth ventricle via the cerebral aqueduct (of Sylvius)

clinical.note: At the foramen of Monro can cause intermittent obstructive hydrocephalus and sudden death.

function: Diamond-shaped ventricle over the pons and medulla receiving CSF from the cerebral aqueduct.
CSF exits to the subarachnoid space through the median aperture (foramen of Magendie) and lateral apertures (foramina of Luschka).

efferent: Central canal of the spinal cord

clinical.note: Fourth-ventricle cystic enlargement with outflow obstruction causes hydrocephalus.

function: The principal dural venous sinus into which CSF is returned to the blood via arachnoid granulations (Pacchionian bodies).
Site of the bulk of CSF reabsorption, completing the circulation from choroid plexus back to the venous system.

efferent: Confluence of sinuses → transverse/sigmoid sinuses → internal jugular vein

clinical.note: Impaired CSF absorption at the arachnoid granulations raises intracranial pressure, causing papilledema and headache.
Sagittal-sinus thrombosis elevates venous pressure, impairing CSF drainage and causing raised ICP.

questions.stem: Where is the majority of cerebrospinal fluid produced?
questions.explanation: The choroid plexuses of the lateral, third, and fourth ventricles secrete ~500 mL of CSF per day via active ion transport.

questions.stem: CSF exits the fourth ventricle into the subarachnoid space primarily through:
questions.explanation: CSF leaves the fourth ventricle through the median aperture (foramen of Magendie) and the two lateral apertures (foramina of Luschka).

questions.stem: CSF is reabsorbed into the bloodstream mainly at the:
options: Arachnoid granulations of the superior sagittal sinus
questions.explanation: Arachnoid granulations project into the superior sagittal sinus and return CSF to the venous circulation.

questions.stem: Find the paired structures that are the principal site of CSF production.
questions.explanation: The choroid plexuses secrete the bulk of cerebrospinal fluid.
